courses.title: CARSI Mould Remediation Practitioner
courses.description:
Prerequisite: CARSI Level 2 Mould Remediation. You must have completed Level 2 to enrol. This is the designation course for the CARSI Mould Remediation Practitioner, a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation at the Practitioner tier (Foundation → Practitioner → Advanced → Master). Level 2 teaches the work; this course assesses whether you can apply it to whole jobs in Australian buildings.

Four modules of integrated Australian case studies: one medium job walked from scope to sign-off, deciding how each area of a building is affected, a common-failure analysis of jobs that came back, writing the defensible job file, and communicating with clients, occupants and insurers. Each lesson points back to the Level 2 lesson it applies rather than teaching it again, and carries a diagram, a worked metric example and a one-page field tool. You then submit a practical task, graded against a five-criterion rubric (pass 70%), and sit the final designation exam (pass 80%). Australian throughout: 230 V / 50 Hz power on a 10 A GPO and RCD, metric units, AUD with GST, and Australian regulators.

The designation is a CARSI credential, separate from IICRC certification. Standards are referenced by name only (for example, AS-IICRC S520:2025).

modules.title: Module 1: The Designation & the Whole Job

lessons.title: The designation: what it requires and how you earn it
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

Priya runs a two-person restoration business in Toowoomba. She finished CARSI Level 2 Mould Remediation last month and has done three mould jobs since. A property manager she wants to work for asks whether she holds a designation, not just a course certificate. Priya wants to know what the CARSI Mould Remediation Practitioner designation asks of her, how it is assessed, and what she has to show that Level 2 did not already test.

The idea

Before you start: this course requires CARSI Level 2 Mould Remediation. You must have completed Level 2 to enrol. Level 2 teaches the work: the inspection route, moisture readings and the drying goal, containment and negative air, respirators and PPE, remove-or-clean decisions, HEPA vacuuming and damp wiping, drying, waste, verification and the job file. This course leaves that teaching to Level 2. Where you need a topic, it names the Level 2 lesson to go back to.

What this course adds is the step from knowing each part to running a whole job and proving it. The CARSI Mould Remediation Practitioner designation is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. CARSI designations run in four tiers: Foundation, Practitioner, Advanced and Master. This one is the Practitioner tier: it says you can take a small or medium mould job in an Australian building from first call to signed-off handover, safely, with evidence a client, occupant or insurer can check.

The course has four modules. Module 1 sets out the designation and walks one job from scope to sign-off. Module 2 is about making the calls on site: deciding how each area of a building is affected, and studying the common failures that make jobs come back. Module 3 is about evidence and people: writing a job file that stands up, and communicating with clients, occupants and insurers. Module 4 is the assessment: you prepare and submit a practical task against a published rubric, then sit the final designation exam.

To earn the designation you need three things. First, Level 2 completed. Second, the practical task passed at 70% or better against its five criteria, graded by a CARSI assessor. Third, the final designation exam passed at 80% or better. The module checks in this course are practice: they help you find gaps before the assessment, and each answer explains why.

Be clear about what the designation is. It is a CARSI credential. It is separate from IICRC certification, which comes only through IICRC-approved schools and examinations, and it is not a pathway to it. Where a standard is relevant, the course names it only. The mould remediation standard is cited as AS-IICRC S520:2025; its detail is taught from the licensed copy by CARSI’s subject-matter expert, and Level 2 covers how it applies on the job.

The law sits underneath every job. The model WHS laws apply in every state and territory except Victoria, where the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 and WorkSafe Victoria apply. Either way, the business carries a primary duty to keep workers and others safe. Go back to Level 2, 1.2 Your WHS duties on a mould job if that is not fresh.

See it

The pathway: Level 2 first, then whole-job case studies, the practical task and the final exam.

Do it in metric

Check whether a job is the right size for the practical task. The practical asks for a medium job, 1–10 m² on the WorkSafe Queensland scale.

  1. Priya’s candidate job: a bedroom wall base 2.8 m long and 0.6 m high, plus a wardrobe back 1.0 m by 0.5 m.
  2. Wall base: 2.8 × 0.6 = 1.68 m². Wardrobe: 1.0 × 0.5 = 0.50 m².
  3. Total: 1.68 + 0.50 = 2.18 m², inside the 1–10 m² medium band. The job suits the task.
  4. Scoring: the practical has five criteria worth 20 points each, 100 in total; 70 points passes. The final exam has 20 questions at 80%, so 16 correct answers pass.

Field download

The Scope-to-sign-off tracker is the one-page record you keep for each job you might submit: stages, dates, evidence held, and the Level 2 lesson behind each stage.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. What must you have completed before enrolling in this course?
  2. A job has 1.68 m² and 0.50 m² of visible growth. Does it suit the practical task?
  3. Is this designation IICRC certification?

Takeaway

Level 2 teaches the work; this course proves you can run a whole job and evidence it. Pass the practical at 70% and the final exam at 80%. Next: one job from scope to sign-off.

Sources for this lesson

  • Safe Work Australia, Model WHS laws. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe Victoria, Information for employers: Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Duties of a PCBU. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe Queensland, Managing mould. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Case study: one job from scope to sign-off
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

A Toowoomba rental, a 1970s brick-veneer house. The tenant reports black spotting on the bathroom ceiling and a musty hall cupboard. The last contractor sprayed and painted; it came back within six weeks. The property manager engages Priya and wants three things: the cause found, the mould gone, and a file she can give the owner and, if needed, the owner’s insurer. Priya has ten working days.

The idea

This lesson follows Priya’s job end to end so you can see how the Level 2 parts join up. At each stage, note the decision she makes, the evidence she records, and the Level 2 lesson it draws on.

Day 1 — first visit and scope. She measures every patch, photographs each against a numbered sketch, records the occupants (one tenant has severe asthma) and asks the year of construction. The house was built in 1974, and homes built before 1990 may contain asbestos, so she books a licensed asbestos assessor before anything is cut. She takes moisture readings from a dry reference outwards and finds the shower recess leaking into the shared wall. (Level 2, 2.1 The inspection route and finding the water; Level 2, 2.2 Moisture readings, dry references and the drying goal.)

Day 2 — the plan. She writes the scope and work plan: areas, containment, negative air, PPE, removal, drying, verification and who signs off. The tenant with asthma is moved out of the affected rooms for the duration, with the manager’s agreement. A plumber is booked for the shower. (Level 2, 2.3 Writing the scope and work plan.)

Days 3–4 — fix and contain. The plumber repairs the recess first, because if the water is not fixed the mould returns. The asbestos result is clear. Priya builds the containment, seals the vents and confirms negative pressure, with every machine on an RCD and the power budget checked at 230 V. Her respirator is fit-tested and she fit-checks it each time. (Level 2, 3.1 Choosing and building containment; Level 2, 3.2 Negative air: how many air scrubbers?; Level 2, 3.3 Respirators and PPE.)

Days 4–5 — remove and clean. The ceiling plasterboard has been wet for weeks and shows growth, so it comes out; SafeWork NSW advises discarding porous materials wet for more than 48 hours or with visible growth. Framing is HEPA-vacuumed and damp-wiped. Waste is sealed in plastic inside the containment and carried out on the planned route. (Level 2, 4.1 Remove or clean? Deciding by material; Level 2, 4.2 HEPA vacuuming and damp wiping; Level 2, 5.1 Bagging and removing waste.)

Days 5–9 — dry. The structure is dried to the reference, with the drying log kept each visit. (Level 2, 4.4 Drying the structure so it does not come back.)

Day 9 — verify. Before the containment comes down she checks that the cause is fixed, the area is visibly clean, materials are at the reference and the air is normal for the house. (Level 2, 5.2 Verification and clearance.)

Day 10 — hand over. The file goes to the manager with a plain-English summary and what the tenant must do to keep the bathroom dry: use the exhaust fan and report leaks early. (Level 2, 5.3 The job file, the client and the assessor.)

The pattern is the point: every stage has a decision, a record and a reason. That is what the practical task asks you to show.

See it

One job, ten days: each stage leaves a record in the file.

Do it in metric

Priya’s numbers for the file. The machine figures are illustrative; use rating-plate and delivered-airflow data for real gear.

  1. Growth: bathroom ceiling 1.6 m × 0.9 m = 1.44 m²; hall cupboard 0.5 m × 0.4 m = 0.20 m²; total 1.64 m² (medium band).
  2. Containment: bathroom and hall end, 2.4 m × 3.0 m × 2.4 m = 17.28 m³.
  3. Air scrubber delivering 400 m³/h (illustrative): 400 ÷ 17.28 ≈ 23 air changes per hour, compared with the job target from her plan.
  4. Power: scrubber 1.8 A + dehumidifier 4.5 A = 6.3 A at 230 V (about 1,450 W), under the 10 A GPO, on an RCD.
  5. Invoice: $1,950.00 excluding GST + $195.00 GST (10%) = $2,145.00 AUD.

Field download

The Scope-to-sign-off tracker mirrors Priya’s ten days: a row per stage with the decision, the evidence held and the Level 2 lesson behind it.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. Why did Priya book the asbestos assessor before cutting anything?
  2. Why does the plumber repair the shower before remediation starts?
  3. A 17.28 m³ containment has a scrubber delivering 400 m³/h. About how many air changes per hour is that?

Takeaway

A whole job is a chain of decisions, each with a record and a reason, from first visit to handover. Next (Module 2): deciding how each area is affected.

Sources for this lesson

  • WorkSafe Queensland, Managing mould. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Government Asbestos, Tradespeople and professionals. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Safe Work Australia, Asbestos overview. Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork NSW, Mould at work. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe ACT, Residual current devices. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Government, Voltage optimisation fact sheet. Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork SA, Fit testing and fit checking of RPE. Read 02/11/2026.
  • enHealth guidance, Potential health effects of mould in the environment (Australian Centre for Disease Control). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Taxation Office, How GST works. Read 02/11/2026.

modules.title: Module 2: Making the Calls on Site

lessons.title: Case study: deciding between conditions across three rooms
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

A ground-floor unit in an older Newcastle block has been empty for three months. The bathroom ceiling has visible growth. The main bedroom next to it has no visible growth but a musty smell and a fine dust on the wardrobe shelves. The kitchen at the far end smells normal and looks clean. The strata manager wants one price for “the mould”. Before Sam, the practitioner, can price it, he has to decide how each room is affected, and write down why.

The idea

Level 2 taught you the condition terms the mould remediation standard uses to describe an area, in Level 2, 1.1 When mould is in the material, not on it, and how they shape the scope, in Level 2, 2.3 Writing the scope and work plan. Go back to both if you need the definitions; this lesson is about using them on a real building, room by room, and defending the call.

Decide each area on evidence, not on impression. For every room, Sam records four kinds of evidence before he decides:

  • What he can see: visible growth, staining, water damage, settled dust, measured in square metres.
  • What he can measure: material moisture against a dry reference, and room air in °C, %RH and g/kg, plus surface temperatures on cold walls.
  • How the room connects: shared doors, a shared air-conditioning return, the direction air moved while the unit was closed up.
  • What he can smell: a musty smell is a reason to look harder, including in cavities.

Apply it to the unit. The bathroom has visible growth, wet ceiling plasterboard and a leaking roof penetration above: the decision is straightforward. The bedroom is the hard call. It has no visible growth, but it shares a door with the bathroom, the wardrobe dust sits downwind of it, and its external wall reads cold. Sam measures the wall at 15 °C with the room at 21 °C and 65 %RH, which puts the wall surface near 95 %RH, so he checks behind the wardrobe and finds growth on the plasterboard behind it. The kitchen has dry readings, no smell and no connection beyond a closed hall door: he records it as his comparison area.

Write the reasoning down. The scope states, for each room, the decision, the evidence and the photos that support it. If an occupational hygienist is engaged, Sam gives them that record. Where the evidence is mixed, he takes the more cautious call and says so, because treating an affected room as clean is the failure that spreads mould to a finished job.

Decide again when the evidence changes. Opening the bedroom wall changed Sam’s view of that room. A change of call is a scope variation: record it, photograph it, and get the client’s written approval before the extra work.

How each call maps to the standard’s own terms is confirmed against the licensed AS-IICRC S520:2025 copy by CARSI’s subject-matter expert.

See it

Each room gets its own evidence panel and a written decision.

Do it in metric

Sam’s cold-wall check in the bedroom.

  1. Room air 21 °C and 65 %RH. Saturation vapour pressure at 21 °C is about 2.488 kPa, so the vapour pressure is 0.65 × 2.488 ≈ 1.617 kPa (about 10.1 g/kg, dew point about 14.2 °C).
  2. At the 15 °C wall the saturation vapour pressure is about 1.705 kPa, so the surface RH is 1.617 ÷ 1.705 ≈ 95 %RH.
  3. That is well above the 70% level the ABCB condensation handbook links with mould growth: a reason to look behind the wardrobe.
  4. Growth found behind it: 1.1 m × 0.6 m = 0.66 m², added to the bathroom’s 1.2 m × 0.8 m = 0.96 m². The unit total rises to 1.62 m².

Field download

The Area decision and failure check has a panel for each room (what you see, measure, connect and smell, then the decision and its reason) and a variation box for a changed call.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. Which four kinds of evidence does Sam record before deciding how a room is affected?
  2. Room air is 21 °C and 65 %RH and a wall reads 15 °C. Roughly what is the RH at the wall surface?
  3. The evidence for a room is mixed. Which way should the call go, and why?

Takeaway

Decide each area on recorded evidence, take the cautious call when it is mixed, and re-decide in writing when the evidence changes. Next: why mould jobs come back.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian Building Codes Board, Condensation in buildings handbook (2023). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Better Health Channel (Victorian Department of Health), Mould and your health. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Common-failure analysis: why mould jobs come back
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

A Brisbane remediation company reviews the last twelve months of callbacks. Six jobs came back with complaints of regrowth, smell or mould in a room that had been clean. The owner wants to know what went wrong, so the same mistakes stop. Reading the six job files side by side, the reviewer finds the same handful of failures again and again.

The idea

Most failed mould jobs fail in the same few ways. Each one below comes from a step Level 2 teaches; the failure is skipping it, doing it out of order, or not recording it. Learn to spot them in your own work and in a file you are asked to review.

1. The cause was not fixed. SafeWork NSW is plain: if the underlying water, moisture or ventilation problem is not fixed, the mould problem will return. In two of the six files the leak was “to be fixed by the owner” with no evidence it ever was. The fix: make the cause repair a sign-off item with a record (invoice, photo, test) before verification.

2. Porous material was kept. One file shows ceiling plasterboard cleaned and painted after being wet for about four days. SafeWork NSW advises discarding porous materials that cannot readily be cleaned, have been wet for more than 48 hours or have visible growth. (Level 2, 4.1 Remove or clean? Deciding by material.)

3. Air was moved before the growth was contained. In one job air movers ran across visibly mouldy skirting on day one. The Northern Territory Government notes that moulds release spores when disturbed, including when a building is being dried out. Mould then turned up in a bedroom down the hall. The fix: containment and negative air first, then removal, then drying. (Level 2, 3.1 Choosing and building containment; Level 2, 4.4 Drying the structure so it does not come back.)

4. Dust was left behind. Two jobs were wiped down but not finished with a final clean; SafeWork NSW advises a final clean-up to remove dust that may have settled within the area or nearby. Queensland Health warns that dry brushing can release spores into the air. (Level 2, 4.2 HEPA vacuuming and damp wiping.)

5. It was rebuilt wet. One file has no reference reading and no final readings, just “dry”. Without a dry reference there is no dry goal, and without readings there is no proof. (Level 2, 2.2 Moisture readings, dry references and the drying goal.)

6. Nobody can show what was done. In every failed file the record was thin. Even where the work was sound, the company could not prove it. (Level 2, 5.3 The job file, the client and the assessor.)

How to use this. Before you sign off any job, run the six questions: Is the cause fixed and recorded? Were porous materials past 48 hours or with growth removed? Was the growth contained before air moved? Was there a final clean? Are final readings at the reference? Could a stranger reconstruct the job from the file?

See it

Six common failures, each traced to the step that was skipped.

Do it in metric

Test two of the failed files against the numbers.

  1. Failure 2: the ceiling got wet on a Monday at 7:00 pm and was cleaned on Friday at 9:00 am. Monday 7:00 pm to Friday 7:00 pm is 96 hours; back to 9:00 am is 96 − 10 = 86 hours, well past the 48-hour mark.
  2. Failure 5: the file’s one drying entry reads 25 °C and 72 %RH in the room, about 14.3 g/kg. The rest of the house read 24 °C and 55 %RH, about 10.2 g/kg. The room was still carrying about 14.3 − 10.2 = 4.1 g/kg more moisture than the house when the wall was closed.
  3. Score the six files against the six questions: if a file fails any one question, it is not ready to sign off.

Field download

The Area decision and failure check carries the six sign-off questions as a tick list, with space for the evidence that answers each one.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. Which failure does SafeWork NSW say makes the mould problem return?
  2. A ceiling was wet for about 86 hours before cleaning. What should have happened to it?
  3. Why does running air movers across visible growth before containment cause callbacks?

Takeaway

Jobs come back for the same six reasons. Run the six questions before every sign-off. Next (Module 3): writing the job file.

Sources for this lesson

  • SafeWork NSW, Mould at work. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Northern Territory Government, Mould growth and your health. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Queensland Health, Mould after a disaster. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Case study: writing the defensible job file
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

Eight months after a remediation in a Geelong rental, the tenant complains that the mould is back and the landlord’s insurer asks for the job file. The technician who did the job has left. What remains is a phone full of photos, a notebook with readings, three invoices and some text messages. The office manager asks Chris, a practitioner, to turn that into a file that shows exactly what was done, and to learn from it so the next file is built properly on the day.

The idea

Level 2 taught what goes in a job file in Level 2, 5.3 The job file, the client and the assessor. This case study is about the craft of writing one that a stranger can follow, and about the difference between a file built on the day and one reconstructed later.

Start with a timeline. Chris puts every item in date and time order: the first call, each visit, each photo, each reading, the plumber’s invoice, the client’s approval texts. Photo metadata gives him times. Gaps show immediately: there are no readings between day 3 and day 7.

Tie every claim to evidence. A defensible file never says “dried” or “cleaned” on its own. It says what was measured, where, with which instrument, against which reference, and points to the photo or log line. Chris’s rule: if a sentence in the summary has no evidence item number next to it, it comes out or is marked as not recorded.

Be honest about what is missing. The missing readings cannot be invented. Chris records them as “not recorded”, and notes what other evidence covers the period (photos showing equipment in place, the hire record). An honest gap is far more credible than a tidy file that looks reconstructed.

Structure it for the reader. The file opens with a one-page summary: the address, the cause and how it was fixed, the areas affected and removed in square metres, the controls used, the verification result and the handover advice. Behind it sit the sections: site reading and scope, cause and moisture map, safety and PPE, containment and daily checks, removal and waste, drying log, verification, communication and approvals, invoices.

Answer the actual complaint. The tenant says the mould is back. The file shows the original leak was repaired (plumber’s invoice), the original area verified dry and clean, and handover advice given to use the exhaust fan. Chris’s site visit finds new growth on a different wall, caused by an unvented clothes dryer installed after the job. The file lets the business show the difference between a failed remediation and a new moisture problem.

What the reviewer decides is up to them. What an insurer, assessor or tribunal accepts is a matter for that body. Your job is to make the facts clear, complete and checkable. Records made at the time, with readings and photos, are the strongest facts you can give them, which is why the next file is built on the day, not afterwards.

See it

Build the file as a timeline; every claim points to an evidence item, and gaps are marked honestly.

Do it in metric

The figures Chris puts in the summary, each tied to an evidence item.

  1. Area removed: wall 3.0 m × 1.2 m = 3.6 m² plasterboard; ceiling 1.0 m × 0.7 m = 0.7 m²; total 4.3 m² (evidence items 12–15).
  2. Final readings at five points: 12, 12, 11, 13, 12 against a reference of 11; average (12 + 12 + 11 + 13 + 12) ÷ 5 = 12.0 (item 31).
  3. Final room air 22 °C and 50 %RH, about 8.2 g/kg, against the hallway at 20 °C and 55 %RH, about 8.0 g/kg (item 32).
  4. Invoices: $2,400.00 excluding GST + $240.00 GST = $2,640.00 AUD, and an approved variation of $380.00 + $38.00 = $418.00 (items 40–42).

Field download

The Job file and communication checklist lists every section of the file, a summary template with evidence-number boxes, and a “not recorded” register for honest gaps.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. What does Chris do with a summary sentence that has no evidence item next to it?
  2. Readings are missing for days 3 to 7. How should the file show that?
  3. Final readings are 12, 12, 11, 13 and 12. What is the average?

Takeaway

A defensible file is a timeline where every claim points to evidence and every gap is marked honestly. Build it on the day. Next: talking to clients, occupants and insurers.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian Taxation Office, How GST works. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Case study: talking to the client, occupants and the insurer
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

A childcare centre in Townsville has a roof leak over a storeroom after the wet season, with growth on the ceiling and stored cardboard. A carer with asthma says her symptoms are worse at work. A parent has emailed asking if the building is safe for children. The centre’s insurer has sent an assessor who wants a scope and a price. Jo, the practitioner, has four audiences and one set of facts.

The idea

Most of a practitioner’s communication is about the same few facts told to different people. WorkSafe Queensland advises communicating with building owners, managers, occupants and tenants about mould issues and treatment work. The skill is giving each audience what they need, accurately, and recording what you told them. Level 2 covers the handover in Level 2, 5.3 The job file, the client and the assessor and health and when to stop in Level 2, 1.3 Health risks and when to stop.

The director (the client). She needs the scope, the timing, the price and what the centre must do. Jo proposes the July holidays, explains containment and access control, and gives a written quote in AUD showing GST. Under the Australian Consumer Law, consumers automatically receive consumer guarantees when they buy services; a clear scope is how both sides know what was promised.

Staff and the carer with asthma. Jo gives no health advice. enHealth lists people with weakened immune systems, allergies, severe asthma or lung diseases as more likely to experience symptoms, and WorkSafe Queensland advises workers at risk of illness from mould to avoid mould-affected areas and notify their employer. So Jo’s message is: the storeroom is closed until the work is finished, please see your GP about your symptoms, and the director has been told.

Parents. The parent wants reassurance. Jo drafts, for the director to send, what is known and what is being done, without promising what cannot be measured. enHealth states there is no exposure limit or health guideline value for mould, so the message avoids the words “safe levels”. It says the affected room is closed, the cause is being repaired, the work happens when children are not on site, and results will be verified before the room reopens. NSW Health’s point that most people will not experience health problems from contact with mould is useful context, and anyone worried about a child’s health should see their GP.

The insurer’s assessor. The assessor needs the cause, the extent in square metres, the method and the evidence plan. Jo separates the insured event (the storm leak) from things outside it (a pre-existing ventilation issue), states what is measured fact and what is opinion, and agrees in writing how variations will be approved. Whether a cost is covered is the insurer’s decision, not hers.

Record it. Every message, who it went to and when, goes in the file. Approvals are in writing.

See it

One set of facts, four audiences, every message recorded.

Do it in metric

Jo’s numbers for the director and the assessor. Rates are illustrative.

  1. Growth: storeroom ceiling 2.2 m × 1.5 m = 3.3 m², a medium job.
  2. Quote: $3,100.00 excluding GST; GST $310.00; total $3,410.00 AUD.
  3. Variation found when the ceiling is opened: a further 1.2 m × 0.8 m = 0.96 m² on the joists, $450.00 excluding GST + $45.00 GST = $495.00, approved in writing by the director and noted to the assessor before work continues.
  4. Prevention advice: the ABCB handbook notes a family of four can generate 7 to 22 kg of water vapour a day; a busy centre adds more, so the advice includes running the storeroom’s exhaust and keeping cardboard off external walls.

Field download

The Job file and communication checklist includes a communication log (who, what, when, how) and an approvals register for scope and variations.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. A carer with asthma asks whether she should keep working near the storeroom. What does Jo say?
  2. Why does the parents’ message avoid the words “safe levels”?
  3. A $450.00 variation is found. What is the total including GST, and what must happen before work continues?

Takeaway

Same facts, tailored to each audience: no health advice, no promised numbers, approvals in writing, every message recorded. Next (Module 4): preparing your practical submission.

Sources for this lesson

  • WorkSafe Queensland, Managing mould. Read 02/11/2026.
  • enHealth guidance, Potential health effects of mould in the environment (Australian Centre for Disease Control). Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Health, Mould (fact sheet). Read 02/11/2026.
  • ACCC, Consumer rights and guarantees. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Building Codes Board, Condensation in buildings handbook (2023). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Better Health Channel (Victorian Department of Health), Mould and your health. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Taxation Office, How GST works. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Preparing your practical submission
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenarios are illustrative; figures labelled illustrative are teaching numbers, and every claim is tracked in the course evidence ledger.

On the job

Ben, a technician in Hobart, has drafted his practical submission from a real job: a bathroom and hallway in a 1960s weatherboard house. He asks a CARSI assessor to look at it before he submits. The assessor reads it against the rubric and marks it as it stands: 62 points. It is a good job, but the submission fails to show it. The fixes are all about evidence.

The idea

The practical task asks you to plan and evidence a medium mould job against five criteria, each worth 20 points, with 70 to pass. The task itself is in this module; read its instructions before you choose a job. This lesson shows how a submission is read, using Ben’s draft.

Criterion 1 — site reading, size and cause. Ben measured the patches but left them untotalled and gave no size band. He found the leak but left out the moisture map’s dry reference, and he made no mention of asbestos, though the house was built in the 1960s. Assessor’s note: show the total, the band, the reference and the asbestos check. Homes built before 1990 may contain asbestos.

Criterion 2 — containment, controls and power. Strong: a sketch, sealed vents, the volume and air changes worked out. Missing: the power budget per circuit at 230 V and the RCD. Assessor’s note: add the amps per circuit.

Criterion 3 — PPE, people and health boundaries. Ben listed “P2 masks”. The assessor wants the respirator type, its AS/NZS 1716 marking, the fit-test date and the fit check, as SafeWork SA requires a fit test before a tight-fitting respirator is first worn. Ben wrote that the occupant’s cough “should clear up once the mould is gone”. That is health advice, and it comes out: the right line is to see a GP.

Criterion 4 — order of work, airflow and verification. Good sequence, but the drying log has no g/kg figures and verification has no readings against the reference. Assessor’s note: show the numbers, not the word “dry”.

Criterion 5 — job file, communication and Australian production. Clear handover advice and pricing in AUD with GST. One US spelling of mould in a photo caption, and one paragraph copied from a product brochure. Assessor’s note: Australian English throughout, own words, standards named only.

Before you submit, run the submission checklist, then read your submission as if you were a stranger: could you rebuild the job from it? Where a decision lacks evidence, add the evidence or explain the gap honestly. Then sit the final designation exam, which tests the whole course and the Level 2 knowledge it applies. You need 80%.

See it

The same job, scored before and after the evidence is added.

Do it in metric

Ben’s draft and revised scores, and the power budget he added.

  1. Draft: 12 + 15 + 11 + 12 + 12 = 62 out of 100, below the 70 pass mark.
  2. Power budget added: scrubber 2.0 A and dehumidifier 4.5 A on the bathroom circuit = 6.5 A at 230 V (about 1,500 W), under the 10 A GPO, on an RCD (illustrative rating-plate values).
  3. Drying log added: inlet 24 °C / 70 %RH, about 13.1 g/kg; outlet 28 °C / 42 %RH, about 9.9 g/kg; a drop of about 3.2 g/kg.
  4. Revised: 17 + 18 + 16 + 17 + 16 = 84 out of 100, a pass.

Field download

The Practical submission checklist lists what each criterion needs to see, so you can check your own submission before an assessor does.

Check yourself

The module check pools three questions on this lesson, each with a practitioner “why” for every answer:

  1. Ben wrote that the occupant’s cough should clear up once the mould is gone. Why must that come out?
  2. A draft scores 12, 15, 11, 12 and 12. Does it pass?
  3. What does the assessor want instead of “P2 masks”?

Takeaway

The practical rewards evidence: totals, references, readings, power, fit tests and honest gaps. Check it like a stranger would, then sit the final exam at 80%.

Sources for this lesson

  • NSW Government Asbestos, Tradespeople and professionals. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe ACT, Residual current devices. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Government, Voltage optimisation fact sheet. Read 02/11/2026.
  • SafeWork SA, Fit testing and fit checking of RPE. Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe Queensland, Respiratory protective equipment (RPE). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Better Health Channel (Victorian Department of Health), Mould and your health. Read 02/11/2026.
